GESTATIONAL CARRIER (SURROGACY) AGREEMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

GESTATIONAL CARRIER AGREEMENT — STATUTORY REQUIREMENTS DECLARATION
This information sheet concerns an assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers, under Cal. Fam. Code §§ 7960-7962, between Jordan Alex LeeTaylor Morgan (the intended parent or parents) and Casey Rivera (the gestational carrier). The parties state, for purposes of the statutory requirements described in this document, that: (1) Casey Rivera is not an intended parent of the child and is not the source of the egg or eggs used, so that the arrangement is gestational rather than traditional surrogacy; (2) Jordan Alex LeeTaylor Morgan and Casey Rivera have each been, or will each be, represented by separate independent licensed attorneys of their own choosing before any assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers is executed; and (3) no embryo transfer procedure, and no injectable medication in preparation for one, has occurred or will occur before that agreement is fully executed and its signatures are notarized or witnessed as required. This information sheet is not itself an assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers and does not itself satisfy, waive, or replace any requirement of Cal. Fam. Code § 7962.

KEY STATUTORY TERMS — "GESTATIONAL CARRIER," "INTENDED PARENT," AND "ASSISTED REPRODUCTION"
California's gestational-surrogacy statute does not actually use the phrase "gestational carrier agreement" as a defined term — the operative contract is defined and referred to throughout Family Code §§ 7960-7962 as an "assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers," built on the more general "assisted reproduction agreement" defined in Family Code § 7606(b) as "a written contract that includes a person who intends to be the legal parent of a child or children born through assisted reproduction and that defines the terms of the relationship between the parties to the contract." "Assisted reproduction" itself means "conception by any means other than sexual intercourse" (§ 7606(a)). Family Code § 7960(c) defines "intended parent" as "an individual, married or unmarried, who manifests the intent to be legally bound as the parent of a child resulting from assisted reproduction" — a definition that is not limited to a married couple, a genetically related person, or any fixed number of intended parents. Section 7960(f) defines "surrogate" as an umbrella term covering two distinct, separately defined categories: a "gestational carrier," meaning "a woman who is not an intended parent and who agrees to gestate a genetically unrelated embryo pursuant to an assisted reproduction agreement," and a "traditional surrogate," meaning a woman who is herself the source of the egg used.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Assisted reproduction” means conception by any means other than sexual intercourse. (b) “Assisted reproduction agreement” means a written contract that includes a person who intends to be the legal parent of a child or children born through assisted reproduction and that defines the terms of the relationship between the parties to the contract."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7606(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), definitions of "assisted reproduction" and "assisted reproduction agreement" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7606.)
  "“Intended parent” means an individual, married or unmarried, who manifests the intent to be legally bound as the parent of a child resulting from assisted reproduction."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7960(c) (California Legislative Information text), definition of "intended parent" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7960.)
  "“Surrogate” means a woman who bears and carries a child for another through medically assisted reproduction and pursuant to a written agreement, as set forth in Sections 7606 and 7962. Within the definition of surrogate are two different and distinct types: (1) “Traditional surrogate” means a woman who agrees to gestate an embryo, in which the woman is the gamete donor and the embryo was created using the sperm of the intended father or a donor arranged by the intended parent or parents. (2) “Gestational carrier” means a woman who is not an intended parent and who agrees to gestate a genetically unrelated embryo pursuant to an assisted reproduction agreement."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7960(f) (California Legislative Information text), definitions of "surrogate," "traditional surrogate," and "gestational carrier" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7960.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines the parties and agreement type in its gestational-surrogacy framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state uses this same terminology or draws its definitions the same way. Whether a jurisdiction recognizes gestational surrogacy agreements at all, and how it defines "intended parent," "gestational carrier," or the agreement itself, varies by state. This clause cites Family Code § 7960(c) and § 7960(f), both subsections of the same statutory section, as well as § 7606(a) and § 7606(b), both subsections of a different statutory section — the two § 7960 citations are treated as one source, not independent, and the two § 7606 citations are likewise treated as one source, not independent, though § 7606 as a whole is an independent source from § 7960. No case law was researched for this clause; the definitions are stated directly from statutory text.

THE STATUTORY REQUIREMENTS FOR A VALID ASSISTED REPRODUCTION AGREEMENT FOR GESTATIONAL CARRIERS
Family Code § 7962 sets out specific, mandatory requirements for the written agreement between a gestational carrier and the intended parent or parents. The agreement must contain, at minimum: the date it was executed; the source of the gametes used (or, if donor gametes were used, whether the donated material was eggs, sperm, or embryos, without necessarily naming the donor); the identity of the intended parent or parents; and disclosure of how the intended parents will cover the medical expenses of the gestational carrier and the newborn or newborns, including — if insurance is used — a review of the policy's coverage for surrogate pregnancy (§ 7962(a)). Before the agreement is executed, the gestational carrier and the intended parent or parents must each be represented by separate, independent, licensed attorneys of their own choosing (§ 7962(b)). The agreement must then be executed by the parties, with signatures notarized or witnessed by an equivalent method as required in the jurisdiction of execution (§ 7962(c)). Critically, the parties may not undergo an embryo transfer procedure, or even begin injectable medication to prepare for one, until the agreement has been fully executed under both the independent-counsel and notarization/witnessing requirements (§ 7962(d)).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers shall contain, but shall not be limited to, all of the following information: (1) The date on which the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers was executed. (2) The persons from which the gametes originated, unless donated gametes were used, in which case the assisted reproduction agreement does not need to specify the name of the donor but shall specify whether the donated gamete or gametes were eggs, sperm, or embryos, or all. (3) The identity of the intended parent or parents. (4) Disclosure of how the intended parents will cover the medical expenses of the gestational carrier and of the newborn or newborns."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(a) (California Legislative Information text), required contents of the agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7962.)
  "Prior to executing the written assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers, a surrogate and the intended parent or intended parents shall be represented by separate independent licensed attorneys of their choosing."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(b) (California Legislative Information text), independent-counsel requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7962.)
  "The assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers shall be executed by the parties and the signatures on the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers shall be notarized or witnessed by an equivalent method of affirmation as required in the jurisdiction where the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers is executed."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(c) (California Legislative Information text), notarization or witnessing requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7962.)
  "The parties to an assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers shall not undergo an embryo transfer procedure, or commence injectable medication in preparation for an embryo transfer for assisted reproduction purposes, until the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers has been fully executed as required by subdivisions (b) and (c) of this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(d) (California Legislative Information text), no embryo transfer or injectable medication before full execution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7962.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California requires for its own gestational-surrogacy agreements to carry the effects described elsewhere in this framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific agreement, nor that every state imposes these same requirements or in this same combination. Whether a gestational carrier agreement is enforceable at all, and what formalities it must satisfy, varies by state. This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section, Family Code § 7962 — subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (d) — which are treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the requirements are stated directly from statutory text. This clause corrects and completes a research-request assumption: the statute's required contents (§ 7962(a)) do not include a psychological evaluation as a stand-alone statutory requirement — that item does not appear in the § 7962 text found here — and this clause does not represent the four items listed as the complete universe of what a well-drafted agreement might address, only the specific minimum content and formalities that § 7962 itself requires by name.

HOW PARENTAGE IS ESTABLISHED — BEFORE BIRTH, AND WITHOUT THE CARRIER BEING A LEGAL PARENT
A properly executed assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers has two distinct legal effects on parentage under Family Code § 7962(f). First, a notarized agreement signed by all parties, with the attorneys' declarations attached and lodged with the superior court, rebuts the marital and other parentage presumptions that might otherwise apply to the gestational carrier or the carrier's spouse or partner (§ 7962(f)(1)). Second, upon petition of any party to a properly executed agreement, the court "shall" issue a judgment or order establishing the intended parent or parents as the legal parent(s) and establishing that the gestational carrier — and the carrier's spouse or partner, if any — is not a parent and has no parental rights or duties with respect to the child (§ 7962(f)(2)). That judgment or order may be issued either before or after the child's birth, and, absent a good-faith, reasonable belief by the court or a party that the agreement or attorney declarations were not properly executed, it issues "forthwith and without further hearing or evidence" (§ 7962(f)(2)) — this is the mechanism sometimes referred to informally as a pre-birth (or pre- or post-birth) parentage judgment. A pre-birth judgment or order is expressly permitted under the general provision governing parentage actions, Family Code § 7633, which allows an action, order, or judgment to be entered before the child's birth, but requires that enforcement of that order or judgment be stayed until the child is actually born.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A notarized assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers signed by all the parties, with the attached declarations of independent attorneys, and lodged with the superior court in accordance with this section, shall rebut any presumptions contained within Part 2 (commencing with Section 7540), subdivision (a) of Section 7610, and Sections 7611 and 7613, as to the gestational carrier surrogate, or the gestational carrier surrogate’s spouse or partner, being a parent of the child or children."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text), agreement rebuts marital and other parentage presumptions as to the carrier (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7962.)
  "the judgment or order shall establish the parent and child relationship of the intended parent or intended parents identified in the surrogacy agreement and shall establish that the surrogate, and the surrogate’s spouse or partner, is not a parent of, and has no parental rights or duties with respect to, the child or children. The judgment or order shall be issued forthwith and without further hearing or evidence, unless the court or a party to the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers has a good faith, reasonable belief that the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers or attorney declarations were not executed in accordance with this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(f)(2) (California Legislative Information text), court-ordered judgment establishing intended parents, before or after birth (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7962.)
  "An action under this chapter may be brought, an order or judgment may be entered before the birth of the child, and enforcement of that order or judgment shall be stayed until the birth of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7633 (California Legislative Information text), pre-birth order permitted, enforcement stayed until birth (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7633.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's framework ties a court judgment to a properly executed gestational carrier agreement, including permitting that judgment before birth — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state offers a comparable pre-birth mechanism or ties it to the same agreement requirements. Whether, and how, a jurisdiction allows parentage to be established before a child's birth through a gestational carrier agreement varies by state. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Family Code § 7962(f)(1) and § 7962(f)(2), which are treated as one source, not independent; § 7633 is an independent source from a different part of the Family Code (the general Uniform Parentage Act determination-of-parentage chapter, rather than Part 7's gestational-carrier-specific provisions). No case law was researched for this clause; the mechanism is stated directly from statutory text.

WHAT HAPPENS IF THE AGREEMENT DOES NOT MEET THE STATUTORY REQUIREMENTS
An assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers that is executed in accordance with Family Code § 7962 is "presumptively valid and shall not be rescinded or revoked without a court order" — but that presumption of validity is itself rebuttable: "any failure to comply with the requirements of this section shall rebut the presumption of the validity" of the agreement (§ 7962(i)). Noncompliance does not, however, automatically defeat the intended parents' claim to parentage. The statute expressly states that it "does not prevent a court from finding and declaring that the intended parent is, or intended parents are, the parent or parents of the child where compliance with this section has not been met"; in that situation the statute requires only that "the court shall require sufficient proof entitling the parties to the relief sought" (§ 7962(f)(2)). In other words, a noncompliant agreement loses the streamlined, forthwith, presumption-rebutting mechanism described elsewhere in this framework, but the statute does not foreclose a court from still finding the intended parent or parents to be the legal parent(s) through ordinary proof.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers executed in accordance with this section is presumptively valid and shall not be rescinded or revoked without a court order. For purposes of this part, any failure to comply with the requirements of this section shall rebut the presumption of the validity of the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(i) (California Legislative Information text), presumptive validity, rebutted by noncompliance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7962.)
  "This section does not prevent a court from finding and declaring that the intended parent is, or intended parents are, the parent or parents of the child where compliance with this section has not been met; however, the court shall require sufficient proof entitling the parties to the relief sought."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(f)(2) (California Legislative Information text), court not barred from finding parentage despite noncompliance, subject to proof (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7962.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California treats a noncompliant gestational carrier agreement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific agreement, nor that every state's framework offers a comparable fallback path to parentage where its own formal requirements are not met. Whether, and how, a jurisdiction treats a noncompliant surrogacy agreement varies by state; some states may treat such an agreement as void or unenforceable without any fallback. This clause corrects a research-request assumption: the statutory text found here does not itself say that a noncompliant agreement is admitted as evidence of the parties' intent in a parentage determination — that specific evidentiary framing does not appear in § 7962's text; what the statute actually says is narrower — that noncompliance is not an automatic bar to a court finding intended-parent status, subject to "sufficient proof." This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Family Code § 7962(f)(2) and § 7962(i), which are treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the treatment is stated directly from statutory text.

COMPENSATION — NOT PROHIBITED, AND FEE HANDLING IS REGULATED WHERE A FACILITATOR IS INVOLVED
California's statutory text does not prohibit paying a gestational carrier for her role, and the statute's own structure assumes money changes hands: Family Code § 7962(a)(4) requires the agreement to disclose how the intended parents will cover the gestational carrier's and the newborn's medical expenses, including a review of insurance coverage for surrogate pregnancy where applicable. Separately, where a "surrogacy or donor facilitator" is involved, Family Code § 7960(b) defines a "fund management agreement" as the agreement between the intended parents and the facilitator covering "the fee or other valuable consideration for services rendered" by the facilitator, and Family Code § 7961 requires that facilitator to direct client funds into either a bonded, independent escrow account or an attorney trust account, disbursed "only ... as set forth in the assisted reproduction agreement and fund management agreement." Nothing in the text of §§ 7960-7962 sets a required dollar amount, cap, or specific structure for what a gestational carrier herself may be paid beyond the medical-expense disclosure requirement described above.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Disclosure of how the intended parents will cover the medical expenses of the gestational carrier and of the newborn or newborns."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), medical expense disclosure requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7962.)
  "“Fund management agreement” means the agreement between the intended parents and the surrogacy or donor facilitator relating to the fee or other valuable consideration for services rendered or that will be rendered by the surrogacy or donor facilitator."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7960(b) (California Legislative Information text), definition of "fund management agreement" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7960.)
  "A nonattorney surrogacy or donor facilitator shall direct the client to deposit all client funds into either of the following: (1) An independent, bonded escrow depository maintained by a licensed, independent, bonded escrow company. (2) A trust account maintained by an attorney."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7961(a), (c) (California Legislative Information text), escrow/trust handling of client funds by a facilitator (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7961.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California does not statutorily bar payment to a gestational carrier and regulates how compensation-related funds are handled where a paid facilitator is used — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state permits compensated gestational surrogacy on the same terms (or at all). Whether compensated gestational surrogacy is permitted, and how any payment must be structured or disclosed, varies significantly by state. This clause draws on three different statutory sections — Family Code § 7962(a)(4), § 7960(b), and § 7961 — each an independent source from the others. No case law was researched for this clause; the absence of a statutory dollar-amount rule and the escrow/fund-management framework are stated directly from statutory text. This clause corrects a research-request framing: the statutory text found here does not itself contain an affirmative sentence declaring compensated gestational surrogacy lawful or not against public policy; the conclusion that compensation is not prohibited rests on the absence of any prohibition in §§ 7960-7962 combined with the statute's own assumption, in the provisions quoted above, that fees and medical costs are paid.

THIS FRAMEWORK COVERS GESTATIONAL SURROGACY, NOT TRADITIONAL (GENETIC) SURROGACY
California's definitions statute expressly distinguishes two categories of surrogate, and the operative agreement statute is written for only one of them. Family Code § 7960(f) defines "surrogate" as an umbrella term with "two different and distinct types": a "traditional surrogate," who is herself "the gamete donor" for the embryo she carries, and a "gestational carrier," who is defined as "a woman who is not an intended parent and who agrees to gestate a genetically unrelated embryo." The requirements and effects set out in Family Code § 7962 — independent counsel, notarization or witnessing, the bar on embryo transfer before full execution, the rebuttal of parentage presumptions, and the forthwith court judgment establishing the intended parent or parents — are all written to apply specifically to "an assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers" (§ 7962(a)), tracking the Part 7 heading itself: "ASSISTED REPRODUCTION AGREEMENTS FOR GESTATIONAL CARRIERS." Nothing in the text of §§ 7960-7962 extends that same mechanism, by its own terms, to an agreement with a traditional surrogate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Within the definition of surrogate are two different and distinct types: (1) “Traditional surrogate” means a woman who agrees to gestate an embryo, in which the woman is the gamete donor and the embryo was created using the sperm of the intended father or a donor arranged by the intended parent or parents. (2) “Gestational carrier” means a woman who is not an intended parent and who agrees to gestate a genetically unrelated embryo pursuant to an assisted reproduction agreement."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7960(f) (California Legislative Information text), "surrogate" as an umbrella term with two distinct types (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7960.)
  "An assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers shall contain, but shall not be limited to, all of the following information:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(a) (California Legislative Information text), agreement requirements scoped to "gestational carriers" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7962.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's own text defines these as two distinct categories and writes its formal agreement mechanism for only the gestational-carrier category — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor a comprehensive statement of what law (if any) governs traditional surrogacy agreements in California. This clause does not resolve, and readers should not assume it resolves, what legal framework — if any — applies to a traditional (genetic) surrogacy arrangement in California; that question is outside the scope of what §§ 7960-7962 addresses, and this clause deliberately does not speculate about it. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Family Code § 7960(f) and § 7962(a) — different subsections of different sections (7960 and 7962) and so treated as independent of each other, while the two definitional sub-parts within § 7960(f) itself are treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the distinction is stated directly from statutory text.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — GESTATIONAL CARRIER AGREEMENT INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on October 15, 2026 at San Francisco, California.

Signature of Intended Parent, Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

Signature of Intended Parent, Taylor Morgan: ☐ _________________________ (if applicable)

Signature of Gestational Carrier, Casey Rivera: ☐ _________________________

Signature of Gestational Carrier's Spouse or Partner, Robin Rivera: ☐ _________________________ (if applicable)

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers, executed under Cal. Fam. Code § 7962 with each party's own independent counsel and with notarized or witnessed signatures. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that agreement, and it does not establish parentage of any child; only a properly executed statutory agreement, together with the resulting court judgment or order described in Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(f), does that. To be filed, if at all, in the county identified as San Francisco County.]

expectedJSON.body: A properly executed assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers has two distinct legal effects on parentage under Family Code § 7962(f). First, a notarized agreement signed by all parties, with the attorneys' declarations attached and lodged with the superior court, rebuts the marital and other parentage presumptions that might otherwise apply to the gestational carrier or the carrier's spouse or partner (§ 7962(f)(1)). Second, upon petition of any party to a properly executed agreement, the court "shall" issue a judgment or order establishing the intended parent or parents as the legal parent(s) and establishing that the gestational carrier — and the carrier's spouse or partner, if any — is not a parent and has no parental rights or duties with respect to the child (§ 7962(f)(2)). That judgment or order may be issued either before or after the child's birth, and, absent a good-faith, reasonable belief by the court or a party that the agreement or attorney declarations were not properly executed, it issues "forthwith and without further hearing or evidence" (§ 7962(f)(2)) — this is the mechanism sometimes referred to informally as a pre-birth (or pre- or post-birth) parentage judgment. A pre-birth judgment or order is expressly permitted under the general provision governing parentage actions, Family Code § 7633, which allows an action, order, or judgment to be entered before the child's birth, but requires that enforcement of that order or judgment be stayed until the child is actually born.

expectedJSON.body: An assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers that is executed in accordance with Family Code § 7962 is "presumptively valid and shall not be rescinded or revoked without a court order" — but that presumption of validity is itself rebuttable: "any failure to comply with the requirements of this section shall rebut the presumption of the validity" of the agreement (§ 7962(i)). Noncompliance does not, however, automatically defeat the intended parents' claim to parentage. The statute expressly states that it "does not prevent a court from finding and declaring that the intended parent is, or intended parents are, the parent or parents of the child where compliance with this section has not been met"; in that situation the statute requires only that "the court shall require sufficient proof entitling the parties to the relief sought" (§ 7962(f)(2)). In other words, a noncompliant agreement loses the streamlined, forthwith, presumption-rebutting mechanism described elsewhere in this framework, but the statute does not foreclose a court from still finding the intended parent or parents to be the legal parent(s) through ordinary proof.

expectedJSON.body: California's statutory text does not prohibit paying a gestational carrier for her role, and the statute's own structure assumes money changes hands: Family Code § 7962(a)(4) requires the agreement to disclose how the intended parents will cover the gestational carrier's and the newborn's medical expenses, including a review of insurance coverage for surrogate pregnancy where applicable. Separately, where a "surrogacy or donor facilitator" is involved, Family Code § 7960(b) defines a "fund management agreement" as the agreement between the intended parents and the facilitator covering "the fee or other valuable consideration for services rendered" by the facilitator, and Family Code § 7961 requires that facilitator to direct client funds into either a bonded, independent escrow account or an attorney trust account, disbursed "only ... as set forth in the assisted reproduction agreement and fund management agreement." Nothing in the text of §§ 7960-7962 sets a required dollar amount, cap, or specific structure for what a gestational carrier herself may be paid beyond the medical-expense disclosure requirement described above.

expectedJSON.body: California's definitions statute expressly distinguishes two categories of surrogate, and the operative agreement statute is written for only one of them. Family Code § 7960(f) defines "surrogate" as an umbrella term with "two different and distinct types": a "traditional surrogate," who is herself "the gamete donor" for the embryo she carries, and a "gestational carrier," who is defined as "a woman who is not an intended parent and who agrees to gestate a genetically unrelated embryo." The requirements and effects set out in Family Code § 7962 — independent counsel, notarization or witnessing, the bar on embryo transfer before full execution, the rebuttal of parentage presumptions, and the forthwith court judgment establishing the intended parent or parents — are all written to apply specifically to "an assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers" (§ 7962(a)), tracking the Part 7 heading itself: "ASSISTED REPRODUCTION AGREEMENTS FOR GESTATIONAL CARRIERS." Nothing in the text of §§ 7960-7962 extends that same mechanism, by its own terms, to an agreement with a traditional surrogate.

citations.quote: Within the definition of surrogate are two different and distinct types: (1) “Traditional surrogate” means a woman who agrees to gestate an embryo, in which the woman is the gamete donor and the embryo was created using the sperm of the intended father or a donor arranged by the intended parent or parents. (2) “Gestational carrier” means a woman who is not an intended parent and who agrees to gestate a genetically unrelated embryo pursuant to an assisted reproduction agreement.
